data.content_ref: inline:The target's central mechanism is factually self-contradictory for an append-only log. It states 'append(event) called twice produces the same log as called once — idempotency,' but an append-only log by definition accumulates entries: appending the same event twice yields [event, event], not [event]. The append operation is therefore NOT idempotent at the log interface. This demolishes the core claim that 'the log must require idempotency (a property it can check and enforce at its abstraction level).' In reality, an append-only event log surviving at-least-once delivery needs writers to provide deduplication identifiers (idempotency keys, unique event IDs) so duplicate deliveries are detected and suppressed — a safety mechanism, not a property that the bare append interface possesses. The target's abstraction-level argument is built on a false premise about what append does. Additionally, the problem explicitly asks to draw on 'published definitions,' and the target provides none — no citations, no research fetches, only self-authored definitions that mischaracterize how safety is treated in the distributed-systems literature (where safety is typically an observable-property concern, not merely an implementation-internal one, as the target's own countercondition 2 concedes).
